name: The medieval banquet as spectacle
strand: The feast & the table through time
scope: The great-hall feast was theatre — every dish a status display. T1: your 'plate' was a trencher, a thick slab of days-old bread that soaked up the juices; diners did NOT eat it — the gravy-soaked trenchers were gathered up afterward as alms for the poor. T2: rank was fixed by the great salt cellar — honoured guests sat 'above the salt' near the host, lesser folk 'below the salt.' T3: a roasted peacock (or swan) was carefully skinned with its plumage intact, cooked, then re-dressed in its own skin and feathers to look alive again — beak and feet gilded gold, sometimes with camphor-soaked cotton lit in the beak so the bird seemed to breathe fire. T4: the boar's head was the ceremonial Christmas centerpiece, carried in on a gilded platter behind trumpeters and dressed with rosemary and bay (the Boar's Head Carol still marks the entrance). T4: there were no forks — a diner brought his own knife, ate with fingers and a spoon, and shared a 'mess' (one plate or bowl split between two or four). T5: because you ate with your hands, servants poured scented water from an ewer/aquamanile to wash hands at the table; and carving was a gentleman's ART with its own verbs (a swan was 'lifted,' a peacock 'disfigured').
source: Grokipedia: Boar's Head Carol. Wikipedia: Trencher (tableware), Boar's Head Carol, Medieval cuisine. English Heritage 'Medieval Christmas Food'; History Skills 'Medieval cuisine' (peacock skinned/re-dressed/fire in beak); medievalcookery.com (trenchers, above/below the salt); Murrey & Blue 'Swan and Peacock in Medieval Recipes'.
framing_note: Prep/spectacle voice is perfect here — lead with the scene ('the peacock is carried in glinting with gold...'), never 'What was a trencher?'. Each rung's answer is one concrete food/table fact (the bread trencher, the re-dressed peacock, the salt divide). ACCURACY RAIL: NO forks at a medieval European table — fingers, knife, spoon, shared mess only. Dinner-test payoff: the peacock re-dressed in its own feathers with its beak breathing fire.

name: Subtleties and sugar at the table
strand: The feast & the table through time
scope: Sugar was once so rare it built edible art. T1: between the courses a 'subtlety' (sotelty) was paraded through the hall — an edible sculpture of a castle, ship, or beast built to astonish the guests. T2: the sculpting medium was marzipan ('marchpane') — ground almonds worked with sugar into a paste you can mold like clay. T3: sugar reached medieval Europe not as everyday food but as a costly MEDICINE and spice sold by the apothecary — so a sugar sculpture flaunted genuine wealth. T4: the word 'banquet' originally named the sweet FINAL course alone — fruits, comfits, marchpane — often taken in a separate little 'banqueting house' after the main meal. T4: coronation subtleties carried political messages — sugar figures and mottoes spelling out allegiances (as at Henry VI's feast). T5: the sugar showpiece faded once Caribbean and Brazilian plantations made sugar cheap and common — the luxury lost its magic when anyone could buy it.
source: Wikipedia: Sotelty (subtlety), Marzipan/Marchpane, Sugar sculpture, Banquet, History of sugar. Murrey & Blue and English-history feast sources (subtleties as sugar/marzipan sculptures between courses). Paul Freedman, food-history background on sugar-as-medicine.
framing_note: Scene-led — 'a sugar castle is wheeled between the courses...'; the answer names the concrete food fact (marzipan = almonds + sugar; 'banquet' = the sweet course). ACCURACY RAIL: sugar in this era = luxury/medicine, NOT the everyday sweetener — do not project modern cheap sugar backward. Keep the plantation beat factual and brief, not a moral essay. Dinner-test payoff: 'banquet' originally meant the DESSERT course.

name: The Roman convivium
strand: The feast & the table through time
scope: Rome's dinner party ran by rules that look alien now. T1: Romans ate lying DOWN — reclining on couches around a low table (the triclinium), propped on the left elbow and taking food with the right hand. T2: myth-bust — the 'vomitorium' was NOT a room for purging so you could eat more; it is the architectural passageway that 'spews' crowds out of an amphitheatre (the Colosseum had 80 of them). T3: Rome's all-purpose condiment was garum — a pungent fermented fish sauce (fish and salt cured in the sun) splashed on nearly everything, their ketchup. T3: a proper dinner had three acts — the gustatio (appetizer, eggs), the main tables, then the sweet finish (fruit, honey): 'from egg to apples.' T4: the trick-dish craze — in Petronius's Trimalchio's feast a hare is dressed with wings as Pegasus and a roast pig spills cooked sausages like innards, dishes built to fool and delight. T5: a status delicacy was the dormouse — fattened in special jars and served glazed in honey and poppy seeds.
source: Grokipedia: Vomitorium. Wikipedia: Vomitorium, Triclinium/Convivium, Garum, Satyricon (Trimalchio's feast), Dormouse (glis glis as food). The Conversation 'Mythbusting Ancient Rome — the truth about the vomitorium'; UNRV 'The Myth of the Roman Vomitorium'.
framing_note: Scene-led — put the reclining diners or a fooling dish in the stem. Every answer is one concrete Roman food/table fact. The vomitorium rung MUST bust the myth cleanly: stem paints the banquet-gluttony image, answer = the exit passage. ACCURACY RAIL: vomitorium = architecture, never a purging room. Dinner-test payoff: the vomitorium myth-bust.

name: The fork's scandalous, slow arrival
strand: The feast & the table through time
scope: The fork was the LAST utensil to reach the table — and it scandalized Europe. T1: for most of history people ate with just three tools — fingers, a knife, and a spoon; there was no fork. T2: when a Byzantine princess brought golden forks to Venice (~1004), a churchman thundered that God already gave us forks — our fingers — and her early death was later blamed on the vanity. T3: Italy took to the fork FIRST, centuries ahead of the rest of Europe, and slippery PASTA is a big reason (you can twirl strands you can't pinch). T4: elsewhere the fork stayed a mocked, effeminate Italian oddity; it became normal across Europe only in the 1700s. T5: dinner knives got their blunt, rounded tips once the fork took over spearing — pointed table knives were discouraged/banned (the famous Cardinal Richelieu story).
source: Wikipedia: Maria Argyropoulina, Fork, Cutlery (rounded table-knife / Richelieu). The Conversation 'The thousand-year story of how the fork crossed Europe'; National Geographic 'How the simple fork almost tore apart the fabric of society'.
framing_note: Scene-led — 'a princess lifts a golden two-pronged tool to her lips and the room gasps...'. Answers are about the eating utensil and the food it served (pasta drove the fork in Italy). ACCURACY RAIL: NO universal fork-dining before the 18th century; frame the Richelieu rounded-knife rung as the traditional account. Dinner-test payoff: the fork condemned as ungodly — 'the devil's tines.'

name: Service a la francaise to service a la russe
strand: The feast & the table through time
scope: How dinner stopped being a spread and became a sequence. T1: in service à la française ALL the dishes arrived at once, crowding the table; you ate what was within reach, so your SEAT decided your dinner. T2: the wow-factor was the SYMMETRY — dozens of dishes laid out in a mirror-image pattern for the eye; partway through, a 'remove' whisked one finished dish away and set down a fresh one. T3: around 1810 the Russian ambassador in Paris, Prince Kurakin — the story goes, after a fire left him unable to reach across the table — had food brought out plated, one course at a time: service à la russe. T4: à la russe is why we now eat in COURSES, and why hot food arrives HOT — each plate is dished up in the kitchen and carried out in sequence. T5: the printed MENU card was born from à la russe — diners could no longer see the whole feast spread before them, so they needed a written list of what was coming.
source: Grokipedia: Service à la russe, Service à la française, Full-course dinner. Wikipedia: Service à la russe (Kurakin, Paris ~1810; spread 1820s–30s), Service à la française. Tasting Table 'The Historical Origins Behind Service à la Russe'.
framing_note: Scene-led — 'forty dishes crowd the table and you can only reach six...'. Answers are about the SERVICE STYLE and its food consequence (courses, hot food, the menu card). ACCURACY RAIL: service à la russe arrived ~1810 and only became dominant across the mid-1800s — do not date modern coursed dining earlier. Dinner-test payoff: à la russe = why we eat in courses (and why the menu card exists).

name: The birth of the restaurant
strand: The feast & the table through time
scope: The modern restaurant was born in Paris — and its origin story is half legend. T1: 'restaurant' first named a FOOD, not a place — a 'restorative' broth, a rich meat bouillon sold to revive the weary. T2: the famous tale credits a Monsieur Boulanger with opening the first restaurant in 1765 selling these broths — but historians (Rebecca Spang's archival work) found no record he ever existed; the real shift was letting a customer CHOOSE a dish, at their own small table, at their own hour, unlike the inn's fixed communal meal at a set time (table d'hôte). T3: the French Revolution (1789) supercharged it — aristocrats fled or fell and their unemployed private CHEFS opened public restaurants, putting palace-grade cooking within reach of anyone who could pay. T4: the à la carte MENU — a written list of individually priced dishes you pick from — was the restaurant's defining invention. T5: the Michelin GUIDE (1900) was created by a TIRE company to get motorists driving to good restaurants (and wearing out tires); its stars became the world's top food rating.
source: Wikipedia: Restaurant (history), Michelin Guide. Rebecca L. Spang, 'The Invention of the Restaurant: Paris and Modern Gastronomic Culture'. National Geographic 'Who Invented the First Modern Restaurant?' (Spang: no evidence Boulanger existed; likely Mathurin Roze de Chantoiseau, c.1767); The Conversation 'Revolutionary broth: the birth of the restaurant'.
framing_note: Scene-led — 'a Paris shop sells cups of restorative broth and calls them...'. Answers are food/dining facts (the broth, the à la carte menu, the tire-company guide). ACCURACY RAIL: the Boulanger-1765 story is a CONTESTED founding legend — frame it as 'the legend says,' and let the solid facts (restaurant = the broth; the Revolution scattered the chefs) carry the rung. Dinner-test payoff: 'restaurant' first meant the SOUP — and Michelin was a tire company.

name: Careme, food as architecture
strand: The feast & the table through time
scope: The pastry chef who made dessert into architecture. T1: Marie-Antoine Carême built towering table centerpieces — pièces montées — shaped like Greek temples, pyramids and ruins, entirely from sugar, marzipan and pastry. T2: he had studied architectural drawings and declared pastry the noblest branch of architecture — his showpieces were literally edible buildings. T3: he is credited with popularizing the vol-au-vent — a tall, hollow puff-pastry case so light its name means 'flying in the wind,' filled with a creamy ragout. T4: he standardized the tall white chef's hat, the toque, and organized grande cuisine's recipes into a system. T5: he cooked for the most powerful of the age (the future George IV, Tsar Alexander, the Rothschilds), earning the title 'the king of chefs and the chef of kings.'
source: Wikipedia: Marie-Antoine Carême, Pièce montée, Vol-au-vent (name attested in F. Marin's 1739 Les Dons de Comus, so 'popularized' not 'invented'). Grokipedia: Pièce de résistance. Kiddle 'Marie-Antoine Carême facts for kids'.
framing_note: Scene-led — 'a three-foot sugar-and-pastry TEMPLE rises from the banquet table — what is it?' but keep the ANSWER food (the pièce montée, the vol-au-vent), never a bare name/date. ACCURACY RAIL: the vol-au-vent name predates Carême — say 'credited with popularizing,' not 'invented.' Dinner-test payoff: the pièce montée — edible architecture.

name: Afternoon tea and the high-tea myth
strand: The feast & the table through time
scope: A duchess's snack became a British ritual — and 'high tea' isn't what people think. T1: afternoon tea — a light spread of tea, finger sandwiches, scones and little cakes around 4pm — was popularized by the Duchess of Bedford to fill the long 'sinking' gap before a fashionably late dinner. T2: myth-bust — 'high tea' is NOT the posh one; it is the hearty working-class hot EVENING meal, named for being eaten at a high dining table (the dainty version is 'low tea,' taken on low parlour tables). T3: the scone ritual splits the country — clotted cream first or jam first (the Cornwall vs Devon method) — a genuinely fought-over order of assembly.
source: British Museum blog 'The tea-rific history of Victorian afternoon tea'. Wikipedia: Tea (meal) / English afternoon tea, Anna Russell, Duchess of Bedford. CNN Travel 'British teatime... sometimes there isn't even any tea' (high vs afternoon/low tea).
framing_note: Scene-led — 'which 'tea' is the hearty hot supper of a working family?'. Answers are food/meal facts (the scone-and-cream spread; which meal each 'tea' names). ACCURACY RAIL: HIGH tea = working-class evening meal; LOW/afternoon tea = the dainty upper-class one — do not swap them. Dinner-test payoff: the high-tea myth-bust.

name: Versailles: dining as theatre
strand: The feast & the table through time
scope: At Versailles even eating was a performance of power. T1: Louis XIV took his main meal in PUBLIC — the grand couvert — while a crowd of courtiers stood and WATCHED him eat, angling for a glance or a word. T2: the kitchens sat so far from the table that dishes made a long, cooling journey — much of the king's food reached him lukewarm. T3: his hunger for the finest produce drove the Potager du Roi, a royal kitchen garden that forced figs, asparagus and peas out of season behind glass and warm walls (gardener La Quintinie). T4: a genuine pea CRAZE gripped the court — courtiers gorged on fashionable petits pois, some (a court lady wrote) eating them again before bed at the risk of indigestion.
source: Wikipedia: Grand couvert, Potager du Roi, Jean-Baptiste de La Quintinie. Château de Versailles 'Royal tables'; Shannon Selin 'Watching French Royals Eat: The Grand Couvert'. Petit pois craze: histoiresroyales.fr and Coquinaria 'A French recipe for 17th-century garden peas' (the Maintenon/Sévigné 'question of peas' letter, 1696).
framing_note: Scene-led — 'the king dines while 300 people stand and watch — what was this ritual?' but keep answers FOOD-anchored where possible (the cold-food logistics, the forced out-of-season produce, the pea craze). ACCURACY RAIL: petits pois were the fashionable luxury vegetable at Versailles — keep the craze factual, attributed to the contemporary court letter, not exaggerated. Dinner-test payoff: the courtiers' pea craze.

name: The buffet and the smorgasbord
strand: The feast & the table through time
scope: The help-yourself table has a Swedish name meaning 'sandwich table.' T1: the 'buffet' — a spread of dishes you serve yourself from a side table — traces to the Swedish smörgåsbord, which literally means 'sandwich-table' (smörgås = buttered bread, bord = table). T2: it began as the brännvinsbord ('schnapps table') — bread, butter, cheese and herring set out with aquavit as a self-serve appetizer BEFORE guests sat down to the main dinner.
source: Grokipedia: Smörgåsbord. Wikipedia: Smorgasbord (smörgås 'buttered bread' + bord 'table'; brännvinsbord origin). Etymonline 'smorgasbord'; ScandiKitchen 'Little Lessons: Smorgasbord'.
framing_note: Scene-led — 'this help-yourself buffet gets its name from a Swedish word meaning what?' Answer = 'sandwich table' (food-anchored etymology). ACCURACY RAIL: the smörgåsbord began as a pre-dinner appetizer/schnapps table, not the whole meal. Dinner-test payoff: buffet = 'sandwich table.'

name: The medieval spice flex and the rotten-meat myth
strand: The feast & the table through time
scope: Medieval spice wasn't flavour rescue — it was showing off. T1: pepper was so valuable it was counted peppercorn by peppercorn and used to pay rents, dowries and ransoms — 'a peppercorn rent' still means a token payment. T2: myth-bust — spices did NOT mask rotten meat; spices were so expensive that only the RICH could afford them, and the rich could equally afford the FRESHEST meat — heavy spicing was a flaunt of wealth, not a cover-up (the rotten-meat idea traces to a 1939 guess by J. C. Drummond). T3: the wealthy medieval palate blended sweet, sour and spice we would now keep apart — cinnamon, ginger, saffron AND sugar all on the same meat dish, before the savoury/sweet split. T4: saffron, the most dazzling seasoning of all, is the hand-plucked stigmas of a crocus flower — which is why a golden, saffron-dyed ('endored') dish shouted luxury across the hall.
source: History Myths Debunked 'Spices were used to mask rotting food' (traces myth to J. C. Drummond, The Englishman's Food, 1939); CulinaryLore and Grunge 'the myth about medieval spices'. Wikipedia: Black pepper (peppercorn rent), Saffron (crocus stigmas). Paul Freedman, 'Out of the East: Spices and the Medieval Imagination'.
framing_note: Scene-led — 'why did rich medieval cooks bury meat in cinnamon, ginger and saffron?'; the ANSWER must bust the myth (to display WEALTH — they could afford both the spice AND fresh meat), NOT 'to hide rot.' Invert-the-wonder on the saffron rung: big colour/luxury in the stem, the crocus flower in the answer. ACCURACY RAIL: the rotten-meat myth is FALSE (a 1939 conjecture) — never endorse it, even as a distractor stem. Dinner-test payoff: the rotten-meat myth-bust.
